anthropocentrism: Anthropocentrism is the view that human beings are the central or most important reality, so that nature, animals, and ecosystems matter mainly insofar as they serve human interests. Many environmental philosophers hold that this human-centered outlook licenses exploitation, and defend alternatives such as biocentrism or deep ecology, which treat the natural world as valuable in its own right.
boethius-consolation: The Consolation of Philosophy is a sixth-century work by Boethius, written while he awaited execution, in which the imprisoned author converses with the figure of Lady Philosophy about fortune, evil, and happiness. Its most famous argument concerns God's foreknowledge: an eternal God stands outside time and beholds all moments at once, so seeing our future choices need not compel them, leaving free will intact.
bushido: Bushido, literally 'the way of the warrior', is the code of conduct associated with Japan's samurai class, emphasizing loyalty, honor, self-discipline, and readiness to face death. Later writers, notably Nitobe in 1899, presented it as a moral philosophy comparable to European chivalry, though historians debate how systematic the code was; following the Hagakure, some stress it was a death-ready mode of action rather than an ethics of right and wrong.
communitarianism: Communitarianism is the view that persons are constituted by their communities: our identities, values, and moral vocabularies come from the traditions, relationships, and shared practices we are born into. On this view, the liberal picture of a self-sufficient individual choosing values from scratch is a fiction, and political life should give due weight to the common good and social bonds, not only to individual rights.
constitutive-rules: Constitutive rules are rules that create an activity in the first place, rather than regulating behavior that exists independently. The rules of chess do not restrict some pre-existing practice; they define what a bishop is and what counts as checkmate, and without them there is no game at all. Philosophers such as Searle used this contrast to explain how institutions like money and marriage are built from shared rules.
democracy-theory: Democracy theory asks what it means for a people to rule itself, and why such rule is valuable. Defenders, like John Stuart Mill, argue that elections force governments to respond and that participation educates citizens; critics from Plato to Marx contend that popular rule invites demagogues or class power. Contemporary work worries that propaganda and misinformation can hollow out democratic legitimacy even where the forms of voting remain.
embodiment: Embodiment is the idea, developed most influentially by the phenomenologist Merleau-Ponty, that we are not pure minds piloting a machine. The lived body is our primary way of having a world: perception, skill, and meaning are bodily achievements. Many hold that this contrasts with Descartes's dualism of mind and body, and it underwrites recent 'embodied cognition' research arguing that thinking depends on the body and environment.
greatest-happiness: The Greatest Happiness Principle is John Stuart Mill's version of utilitarianism: actions and institutions are right insofar as they promote the greatest happiness for the greatest number, understood as pleasure minus pain. Mill added that pleasures differ in kind, so intellectual and emotional pleasures count for more than bodily ones, judged by those experienced in both. It remains the classic yardstick for measuring laws and policies by their consequences.
hegel-geist: Geist, or 'Spirit', is Hegel's name for the collective mind of humanity as it develops through history. On his view, cultures, conflicts, and world-historical individuals are the instruments by which Spirit gradually comes to know itself, and history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. Opposing forces, such as tradition against modernity, drive this development rather than merely obstructing it.
hume-sentimentalism: Hume's sentimentalism is captured in his slogan that 'Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions.' Moral judgment, he argued, is grounded in feeling, not rational proof: we approve or condemn because of sentiment, and reason's job is only to work out means to the ends our desires set. Many subsequent metaethicists have developed or contested this sentiment-based picture of morality.
invisible-hand: The invisible hand is Adam Smith's metaphor for how individuals pursuing their own self-interest in competitive markets can unintentionally promote the public good, as if guided by an unseen force. Often quoted as a blanket defense of markets, the phrase appears only briefly in Smith's writings, and many scholars stress that for him it operated within the constraints of justice, not instead of them.
machiavelli-ends: 'The ends justify the means' is the doctrine popularly attributed to Machiavelli's Prince: a ruler may do wrong when necessity demands it, and actions should be judged by their results for the state rather than by private morality. Machiavelli wrote that the prince must learn 'how not to be good', and readers still debate whether the book is sincere advice for rulers or a veiled exposure of their methods.
machiavelli-virtu: Virtù and Fortuna are Machiavelli's two great forces in politics. Virtù is not virtue in the moral sense but the skill, boldness, and adaptability a ruler needs to impose his will on events; Fortuna is luck and circumstance, a river that floods unless dikes are built. On his view fortune governs perhaps half of our actions but favors the prepared and daring, who can master her.
macintyre-tradition: In After Virtue, Alasdair MacIntyre argues that modern moral debate has lost its shared framework, leaving fragments of incoherent argument. His reconstruction holds that virtues are acquired through 'practices', cooperative activities like chess, farming, or science that have internal goods, standards of excellence proper to the activity itself rather than external rewards like money or fame, and that these practices are sustained and made meaningful within living traditions.
moral-egoism: Ethical egoism is the theory that each person ought to act in their own self-interest. It is distinct from psychological egoism, the empirical claim that everyone inevitably does act selfishly. Critics object that it cannot explain ordinary duties to others, while defenders, most famously Ayn Rand, hold that rational self-interest actually requires honesty and respect for other people rather than predation.
moral-relativism: Moral relativism is the view that the truth of moral judgments is relative to a person or culture, so that there is no single universal standard: what counts as right is right for a given framework. Critics argue it makes cross-cultural criticism impossible and dissolves genuine disagreement, since simple subjectivism would make every judge infallible. Defenders point to deep cultural disagreement and to respect for other ways of life.
pascals-wager: Pascal's Wager is Blaise Pascal's argument that, since reason cannot settle whether God exists, we should believe anyway as a bet: if God exists, belief wins infinite happiness, while if he does not, we lose little. Philosophers have objected that we cannot simply choose to believe, that it does not say which God to bet on, and that belief should be proportioned to evidence.
power-knowledge: Power/knowledge is Michel Foucault's term for the intimate tie between knowledge and power. What counts as true, he argued, is shaped by institutions such as medicine, the prison, and psychology, and that knowledge in turn disciplines people, classifying them as sick, mad, or criminal. Power on this view is not simply possessed by rulers but circulates through networks, producing the very subjects it governs.
social-darwinism: Social Darwinism is the application of biological ideas like 'survival of the fittest' to human societies, used to justify inequality, imperial conquest, or eugenics as natural and inevitable. Many historians note the term is loose: Darwin himself distinguished natural selection from deliberate breeding and never endorsed these politics, and philosophers commonly treat social Darwinism as a misreading of evolution, since natural selection describes what happens, not what ought to be.
sun-tzu-strategy: Sun Tzu's Art of War, a Chinese military classic from roughly the fifth century BCE, teaches winning with minimal conflict: through deception, formlessness, knowing the enemy and oneself, and ideally winning without fighting at all. Its deepest strain, many argue, rests on a vision of harmony and interdependence rather than sheer aggression, which is why the book is read today well beyond warfare, in business, sport, and negotiation.
the-uncanny: The uncanny, Freud's das Unheimliche, is the class of frightening things that are strangely familiar: the homely turned unhomely. Freud argued its horror comes from the repressed returning to light, in figures such as doubles, lifelike automatons, and the returning dead. This explains why beings that resemble us too closely, like Frankenstein's creature, can terrify more than obvious aliens.
will-to-believe: The Will to Believe is William James's defense of faith where evidence cannot decide the question. When an option is live, forced, and momentous, as in trusting other people or in moral and religious commitments, James held that our passional nature may legitimately choose, since suspending judgment is itself a choice with risks. He did not license wishful thinking about ordinary facts, only belief where evidence is neutral.
woman-as-other: In The Second Sex, Simone de Beauvoir argues that men have been treated as the default human Subject, while woman is constructed as the Other, defined relative to man rather than as a self-defining person. Her famous claim that one is not born but becomes a woman holds that femininity is a social creation, and that women's liberation must be won through independent action, not merely granted by men.
yin-yang: Yin and yang are the complementary opposites of Chinese cosmology: dark and light, receptive and active, which exist in dynamic balance and each contain the seed of the other. Neither force is good or evil; on this view, excess of either brings destruction, and harmony lies in balancing and moving between them. The symbol of two interlocking drops, each holding a dot of its opposite, expresses this interdependence.
